text: Feasibility, optimality, ordering, symmetry and repeated-state cuts.

A plain DFS (基础篇第14章) visits every branch. Pruning (剪枝) proves early that a branch cannot lead to a (better) answer and cuts it off. Good pruning often turns "never finishes" into "a few milliseconds"; the answer stays the same.

Kind of pruning Cut a branch when … Example feasibility the remaining choices can no longer reach a valid answer the sum left is too large to fill optimality the cost so far already reaches the best answer found path length ≥ best order of choices (not a cut) try the most constrained or largest choice first, so failures come early sort sticks longest first repeated states the same state was already explored memo / visited set symmetry a branch is a mirror of one already tried equal sticks: try one, skip the rest

Rebuilding broken sticks (P1120) needs every kind of cut: the original length divides the total; pieces are tried longest first and in increasing index (no reordering of the same stick); a failed length is not retried; if the first piece of a new stick fails, or a piece that exactly finishes a stick fails, no other choice can work, so the whole branch returns false.

Optimality pruning: once a full route of length best is known, any partial route already that long is abandoned. The better the first answer found, the more is cut, which is why visiting nearer pieces first can help (P1433).

For n up to 15 the safe method is a state over "which pieces are eaten" (状态压缩 , 第17章); pruning only makes plain DFS fast on typical data. Sudoku-like puzzles (P1074) fill the cell with the fewest options first.
IDDFS for shallow answers; meet in the middle for 2ⁿ splits.
depth ≤ 1 depth ≤ 2 depth ≤ 3 rerun DFS with a growing depth limit until it succeeds

Iterative deepening (迭代加深 , IDDFS): run a DFS that refuses to go deeper than D; if it fails, try D + 1. The first D that succeeds is the shallowest answer, like BFS, but memory stays as small as DFS. The repeated shallow levels cost little because the deepest level dominates.
Use it when the answer is shallow but the tree is wide or infinite in depth: plain DFS would wander deep and never return, and BFS would need too much memory.

Shortest addition chain: start from 1, each new number is the sum of two earlier ones, reach n with the fewest additions. The depth is small (about 2 log₂ n) but every level has many choices, a perfect fit for iterative deepening.
The doubling test is an estimate of the steps still needed: even doubling every time cannot reach n, so stop. Egyptian fractions (P1763) use the same "deepen, estimate, cut" pattern.

240 subsets are far too many, but 2 × 220 ≈ 2 million half-subsets are fine. Meet in the middle (双向搜索 / 折半搜索): enumerate each half separately, sort one side, and count matching pairs with binary search (P4799).

The pattern works whenever the answer is "a choice from the left half combined with a choice from the right half": sums (CF525E with factorials), products below a bound (CF912E). Searching from both ends of a graph toward each other is the same idea.
A* with an estimate that never overestimates; IDA*.

Heuristic search (启发式搜索) uses an estimate h(state) of the remaining cost to explore promising states first. A*: always expand the state with the smallest f = g + h, where g is the cost so far. If h never overestimates the true remaining cost, the first time the goal is taken from the queue its cost is optimal.

A good h is cheap to compute and as close to the truth as possible without exceeding it. For sliding puzzles, "how many tiles are out of place" and "total Manhattan distance of the tiles" both never overestimate.

The board is a 9-character string, the queue is ordered by g + h, and map<string, int> keeps the best known cost of every state (P1379). Plain BFS explores states in every direction; A* heads toward the goal.
With a memory limit, IDA* runs iterative deepening with the bound "g + h ≤ D" instead (knights P2324, the mechanism puzzle P5507).
An h that sometimes overestimates can make A* return a non-optimal answer. When unsure, take a weaker estimate; h = 0 turns A* back into ordinary shortest-path search.
